rationale: How much signal each drug carries varies a lot: targeted oncology drugs have strong expression markers, while many non-oncology drugs are mostly noise. One shared alpha=5000 therefore over-shrinks some drugs and under-shrinks others. This change keeps the same features and lets RidgeCV pick a separate penalty for each drug. It does this with leave-one-out cross-validation on the training fold only (one cell line per item), using the fast closed-form solution, so it costs about the same as a single ridge fit.

A large share of PRISM drug sensitivity is driven by lineage, but a single heavily penalised ridge (alpha=5000) over 5,000 genes can only pick up lineage weakly, through many shrunken gene weights. This change first fits a shrunken per-lineage mean for each drug (an empirical-Bayes blend toward the drug's overall mean, using only observed AUCs). It then fits the same ridge on the residuals and adds the lineage baseline back at prediction time.

PRISM AUCs share a lot of low-rank structure across drugs (a general cytotoxicity/sensitivity axis plus a few MOA-specific axes). So I replace the independent per-drug ridge with a reduced-rank ridge: per-drug predictions are projected onto the top-k principal directions of the fitted drug-response matrix, which lets drugs share strength and filters out drug-specific noise. k is chosen by inner grouped CV on the training fold.

Many PRISM drugs, especially targeted oncology drugs, have a direct biomarker: the expression of their own target genes. Inside a 5,000-gene ridge with alpha=5000, those genes are diluted or missing altogether. This change adds the expression of all annotated drug-target genes (the union across the 200 drugs) as extra standardized columns. They are multiplied by a weight w, and since ridge penalizes coefficients, scaling a column up by w cuts its effective penalty by w². w is picked from {0, 2, 4, 8} by grouped 3-fold CV on the training fold only, scored by mean per-drug Pearson r; w=0 means no target features, so it can fall back to the current model.

The shared ridge uses the same 5,000 variance-filtered genes for every drug, so the strong individual markers of targeted drugs get diluted (the target-gene columns tried in round 4 didn't fix this). This change adds a second model per drug: it picks that drug's top-k most correlated genes from a wider pool, using observed AUCs in the training fold only, fits a ridge on them, and blends it with the current ridge as z-scored predictions. The values of k, the penalty and the blend weight (w=0 means the current model alone) are chosen by grouped 3-fold inner CV on the training fold, scored by mean per-drug Pearson r.

Many of the 200 PRISM drugs share a mechanism (several MEK, EGFR or HDAC inhibitors, for example), and their AUC profiles across cell lines are strongly correlated. So I average each drug's noisy blended prediction with the predictions of its most similar drugs. The drug-drug similarity comes from response correlations in the training fold, which should cut per-drug variance. The smoothing strength g is picked by grouped inner CV along with k, the penalty and the blend weight. Each inner fold uses a similarity matrix built only from its own training rows, and g=0 falls back to the current model.

For drugs with weak signal, picking the top correlated single genes is noisy. Averages of z-scored member genes over Hallmark and Reactome gene sets are less noisy markers of biology such as MAPK, interferon, EMT and proliferation. This change computes those gene-set scores without labels in `featurize` and adds them to the candidate pool that the per-drug correlation-selected ridge picks from. The shared ridge still uses genes only, and inner CV still picks k, the penalty, the blend weight and the smoothing strength. If no GMT files are found, the model falls back to the current behaviour.

This adds a third component: an RBF kernel ridge fitted to all 200 drugs at once, over cell-line similarity in the top-5k variable genes. Similar cell lines, such as lines from the same lineage or with a shared transcriptional state, tend to respond alike in non-linear ways that the two linear ridges miss. Grouped inner CV on the training fold picks the kernel penalty and blend weight together with the existing k, penalty, blend weight and smoothing strength; a kernel weight of 0 falls back to the current model.

For drugs with weak signal, ranking genes by correlation with that one drug's noisy AUC picks unstable markers. This change averages each drug's gene-correlation profile with those of its response-correlated neighbour drugs (same weights as the existing smoothing) before choosing its top-k genes. The ridge is still fitted to the drug's own AUCs. The sharing strength a ∈ {0, 0.5} is picked by grouped inner CV along with the other settings, and a=0 falls back to the current model.

Picking one (k, λ) gene-panel configuration through a noisy 3-fold inner CV adds selection variance. Round 9 showed that even extra grid options with a fallback can lose score. So I replace the single pick with an even average of the z-scored per-drug ridges over a wider multi-scale grid (k ∈ {50…1000} × three penalties), a bagging-like ensemble of marker panels. Inner CV now only chooses the blend weight w and the drug-smoothing strength g.

Some drugs have strong single-gene markers (targeted oncology agents) and others have mostly diffuse signal, yet every drug currently uses the same base/filtered blend weight. This change also picks a blend weight for each drug from the existing inner out-of-fold predictions, then pulls it toward the global weight by a shrinkage factor s ∈ {0, 0.5, 1}. To keep s honest, each inner fold is scored with per-drug weights chosen on the other folds only, and s=0 falls back to the current model.

The shared ridge is the only part of the model that still uses a single hand-picked setting (top 5,000 genes, alpha = 5,000). This change replaces it with an even average of z-scored multi-output ridges over three gene-pool sizes (2k, 5k, 10k) and three relative penalties (alpha = a·p). Averaging over panel sizes and penalties helped the per-drug component in round 10, so the same should help here, and the dual (kernel) form keeps it cheap: one eigendecomposition per pool covers all penalties and all 200 drugs.
